lesson.title: S Phase: Copying the Entire Genome
lesson.summary: S phase, short for synthesis phase, is when the cell replicates its entire DNA content, duplicating each chromosome into two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.
lesson.body:
S stands for "synthesis," and S phase is when a cell does the single most information-dense task in its entire life cycle: copying its entire genome. Every chromosome that entered S phase as a single strand of DNA leaves S phase duplicated into two identical sister chromatids, physically held together at a region called the centromere by proteins called cohesins. It is important to be precise about what does and does not change here. The chromosome number itself does not increase during S phase, a cell that had 46 chromosomes in G1 still has 46 chromosomes right after S phase, because each duplicated chromosome, sister chromatids and all, is still counted as one chromosome until those chromatids are physically pulled apart later in mitosis. What does change is the total amount of DNA in the cell, which doubles, since every chromosome now contains two identical copies of its genetic information instead of one.

Copying the genome accurately is an enormous undertaking. Replication starts at many points along each chromosome simultaneously and proceeds in both directions from each of those starting points, with specialized enzymes unwinding the DNA double helix and building a new, complementary strand alongside each original strand. This process has to be both fast enough to finish within S phase and accurate enough that errors are rare, since any mistake copied into a chromosome will be passed on to a daughter cell and, ultimately, to every cell descended from it.

S phase sits in the middle of the cell cycle for a reason: it depends on having passed the G1 checkpoint discussed previously, which confirms the cell is ready to commit resources to replication, and it sets up the checks that come next in G2, which will verify that replication actually finished correctly before the cell is allowed to proceed into mitosis. In that sense S phase is bracketed on both sides by quality control, a reflection of just how costly it would be to get genome duplication wrong.
